toc.title: One: your own nervous system state
Three: your expectations and the stories you tell

blocks.p: I spend a lot of time talking about shutdown: how to recognize it, work with it, and even move through it. Usually I talk to you as if you are the one in shutdown. Here I want to flip things a little and talk about what it's like to be with someone who's in shutdown. Specifically, what it's like to be their partner, and what you can and cannot do about it.

If you're with someone who is in a dorsal vagal shutdown, you're not just watching it happen. You're in it too, in your own way. Your experience is real, and it's confusing and frustrating, and it's okay to talk about it without judgment, without blame, and without pretending that what you're feeling doesn't matter.
So this is for the partners out there. The ones who feel like they're losing their person. The ones who don't understand what's happening. The ones who feel like maybe they're making it worse.
I'll start by describing what I think many partners experience when someone they love is in shutdown, depending on the severity, of course.

Sometimes it might seem like they're not quite there. Their eyes look different, or blank, or maybe even lifeless. They're not moving, or they're moving slower. They're not responding the way they used to. They lack energy for life, or it comes and goes in spurts. When energy is there, it's spent on time wasters like video games and doom scrolling social media. Or they come out of shutdown enough to be irritable, then go right back into it. They might not be meeting basic life responsibilities around work, self-care, family, and social life.

If you know about the nervous system and understand the Polyvagal Theory's autonomic state shift sequences, you might recognize what's happening in your partner. If that describes them, they're in shutdown. But then sometimes they're not, because all of a sudden they have energy. And then they're shut down again.

Knowing what your loved one's shutdown is doesn't necessarily make it easier to deal with, obviously. You might be witnessing anything from full-on dissociation to someone just lacking the motivation to take care of the household chores. It might feel like they're not fully there anymore, and that can feel like losing them in a sense, even if they're sitting right in front of you.
Judgmental thoughts might pop into your head: this person doesn't care. They're not trying hard enough. They're resistant, they're apathetic, they just want to isolate and hide.

You might be taking on unnecessary guilt, like blaming yourself for your partner's shutdown. Maybe you think you're making it worse somehow, or that you're not good enough for them to come out of shutdown.

All of this, the judgment about them and about yourself, just adds friction to the process. It doesn't help them and it doesn't help you, and I'm sure you're aware of that. You're not choosing to have these thoughts and feelings. They're just kind of there. So there's no blame from me. I'm just calling it out. We have to tell the truth about these things and acknowledge what's happening. These stories in your brain are not true. We both know that. We'll come back to them.

Let's review what we're talking about. Dorsal vagal shutdown is a Polyvagal Theory term. It's a biological state. It's what happens when your nervous system perceives a life threat or overwhelm and decides that the best protection is to go offline: to conserve energy, to dissociate, maybe to become still and quiet or away somewhere. It's an immobilized collapse in the face of a life threat. Not a conscious choice, but a brainstem, autonomic nervous system level, biological occurrence.

Shutdown looks like depression. In the Polyvagal Theory, this state is probably what underlies the depression label, the diagnosis, and it's how I personally view it with my therapy clients: low energy, task avoidance, anhedonia, isolation, dissociation. Shutdown and depression seem to me to be kind of the same thing, but shutdown is an actual explanation, versus just labeling somebody.

The person in shutdown isn't choosing it. They can't just snap out of it because you asked them to, or begged them to, or because logically they know they should come out of shutdown. That's not the way it works. Their nervous system is in a protective state, and that's not something willpower or external force can change.
So let's talk about what you, as the partner of someone in shutdown, can and cannot do.

First, you cannot regulate your partner out of their shutdown state. You cannot force them out of it. You cannot think them out of it. You cannot love them out of it. You cannot be patient enough, present enough, or good enough to make it end. Their shutdown is theirs. It belongs to their nervous system, their history, their context, their capacity. That's not something you have power over.

Similarly, you don't control how long it lasts. Some shutdowns are brief. Some linger. Some cycle. That duration is not determined by how well you show up. It's determined by their system's readiness to shift, and that's on their timeline, not yours.

Second, you can't control whether they do their own trauma recovery, self-development, or unstucking work. You can't force them into therapy, into self-regulation practices, into nervous system awareness. You can't make them want to change or heal. That has to come from them, ultimately.

I think a lot of partners carry a hidden belief that if they just do enough, say the right thing, offer the right kind of presence, sacrifice enough, then their person will get better. That's probably a setup for burnout and resentment, because it puts the responsibility for their healing on your shoulders. It probably sounds absurd as I say it. If someone you knew told you they had put it on themselves to fix their partner, you'd probably raise your eyebrows in some nervous disbelief.

To put it plainly: your partner's recovery out of shutdown is ultimately not on your shoulders. Their nervous system, their shutdown, their timeline, their willingness to engage with their own unstucking process: that is ultimately all theirs.

That plain truth might feel cold, or like I'm saying you don't matter. That is not it at all. What I'm saying is, let's be honest about the boundaries of your influence, so that you can actually be effective in the ways that do matter.

You are part of their life, so even though you don't control them, you of course have influence. Think of yourself and your partner as two cogs in a two-cog machine, spinning in the same direction forever. If one of you acts differently, the other one must as well. If one of you refuses to turn in the same direction, the other must respond differently. They have to.

While you can't control their shutdown, there's quite a bit you can control that will have influence on them. Control them? No. Fix them? No. Make them come out of shutdown? No. But are there things you can do to increase the likelihood they may start the process of exiting shutdown? Yes, I think there are. I'll address four of them broadly.
I'm sure you'll hear some of these and say, "Yes, but..." many times. I don't know your life, and it's up to you to adapt these ideas to your own life, if you want to.

blocks.h: One: your own nervous system state

blocks.p: This is huge. When your partner is in shutdown and you're getting frustrated, impatient, disappointed, or shutting down along with them, your body is sending a signal, and your partner feels it. They might not be able to articulate it, but their system is picking up your activation, or your lack of it, and that could make it harder for them to shift out of shutdown.

It's not your fault, of course. But in times like this, it's important to regulate yourself in whatever way you know works best. Step outside, do a breathing exercise, flex and release to use any activation within you. It doesn't really matter. Do what works best for you. Regulating yourself may help your partner because it doesn't add friction to the process. Your partner has their own shutdown to deal with. They don't need your judgment on top of it.

You're absolutely allowed to have your own thoughts and feelings about your partner's shutdown. You can feel disappointed, frustrated, fed up, and more. Those are your feelings, and they are real. In no way am I asking you not to feel them. Can we agree on that? When you have these feelings, it's up to you to deal with them, not your partner. So take the time to regulate yourself as best you can, when you can.

You also don't need to keep these feelings to yourself. You're allowed to voice them to your partner. I'm in no way asking you to keep your feelings a secret. I think it's very important for your loved one to know what you're going through, if they're open to hearing it. And honestly, sometimes you may need to express your feelings even if they're not open to hearing it, because it just needs to be said.

However, I encourage you to express your emotions and thoughts from a regulated state. You don't have to be calm and happy. You can be upset. You can be frustrated and disappointed and whatever else. I want you to speak and listen with compassion for yourself and your partner. I want you to speak and listen with empowerment, not out of controlled anger. I want you to speak and listen with truth telling, not shaming and blaming.

Yes, your partner is affecting your life with the decisions they make from their shutdown. Whether or not it's intentional is irrelevant. You're allowed to tell them how they impact you if you want to. That's one way the cog in the two-cog machine stops spinning in the same direction and chooses to do something different.
I want you to look at self-regulation in two ways.

The first is in response to your partner's decisions. You feel something, and then you regulate through it. This helps decrease the intensity of what you're going through, and it can help to simmer the situation down, which is better than nothing.

The second way is through your own practices to become a self-regulated person. It's the stuff you do not because of your partner, but because you want to be a more self-regulated person. Practices like simple daily mindfulness help to create a regulated baseline that you bring to every area of your life, including your partner. This second way is very proactive. It's not in response to your partner, or something that happened at work, or your parents. You're practicing self-regulation just to be a self-regulated person.

If you're doing this, your partner's decision making will still impact you, but less intensely. And when you do address it, you'll do so with more empathy, compassion, and empowerment, and also honesty.

Does being a self-regulated person cure their shutdown? No. That is still out of your control. But it can open the potential for them to begin to come out of shutdown, because much of the friction of judgment, shame, and blame is at least lessened. And you'll be offering more co-regulation opportunities, which we'll get to. It's still up to them ultimately, but your level of regulation, and the decisions you make in the relationship as the cog that refuses to turn in the same direction, could nudge them indirectly toward some kind of change.

The second thing you can control is your boundaries. You get to decide how much space you need. You get to decide which tasks you're willing to carry and which ones you're not. You get to decide when you need to step back for your own sake. You get to decide how much physical and emotional labor is sustainable for you. You can say no to some things and not to others.

Clear boundaries are not selfish. For example, saying, "I can help with the dishes tonight, but I need you to do the laundry tomorrow when you're feeling more present," is a healthy boundary. Saying "I'll do everything, the dishes, the laundry, your work emails, all of it, because you're in shutdown" is an unhealthy boundary, and now it's at your expense.

Again, clear boundaries are not selfish. Saying, "I won't send that email to your boss for you, but I can proofread it when you're done," is a healthy boundary. Saying, "Sure, I'll call your supervisor and explain why you're not coming in," crosses into territory where you're now responsible for managing their professional consequences.

Healthy boundaries are about supporting without taking over. The other kind is about absorbing their accountability and responsibility, which actually prevents them from finding their own agency, and can create resentment when it becomes a pattern. Unhealthy boundaries, where you take on more than you probably should, only reinforce the behavior and decisions of the other person, whether they're in shutdown or not. Be the cog that refuses to turn, and the other one must do something different.

Boundaries are essential to your self-regulation efforts. If you're sacrificing everything, if you're running on empty, then you're not actually available in the way that matters. Unclear boundaries lead to resentment and depletion that don't help anyone. Taking care of your own boundaries is how you stay present. It's how you sustain yourself. And paradoxically, it can help influence the other person to find their own agency and start making changes, even small ones. And small changes are actually really good for shutdown.
Again, you don't control your partner in shutdown, but your decisions, what you do or do not take on, will influence their decision making.

blocks.h: Three: your expectations and the stories you tell

blocks.p: The third thing you can control is your expectations and the stories you tell. Well, kind of. I don't think we exactly control our thinking, sorry to all the mindset gurus. But we can at least be more aware of our thinking and challenge it, especially if we're more self-regulated than not.

Are you expecting them to regulate quickly? Are you expecting them to snap out of it because you've been patient long enough? Are you personalizing their shutdown, thinking it's about you? That they're rejecting you? That if they really loved you, they'd be more present?

Those stories shape how you show up. You get to catch them, examine them, and maybe even shift them. When you notice these thoughts, don't reject them. Just notice them, and maybe reflect on what you're feeling. Journal about these thoughts if you like, but prioritize your emotions in the present moment as you're processing.

The fourth thing you can control is what you communicate. You get to be honest. You get to say, "I'm struggling with this too." You get to ask, "What do you need from me right now?" You get to offer presence without demand. You get to set expectations: not demands, but honest clarity about what you can and can't do.

You don't have to pretend it's easy. You don't have to pretend to be fine. You can be real, and sometimes that realness is actually more settling, more safe, for the person in shutdown than trying to be perfect.
You've probably heard the word co-regulation in the Polyvagal Theory world. I think it's misunderstood in general.

Co-regulation doesn't mean you intentionally regulate them. It doesn't mean your presence alone will shift their state. It doesn't mean that if you're calm enough, present enough, attuned enough, they'll come out of shutdown. Co-regulation isn't exactly a tool you get to use to get the outcome you want. If you're attempting to use co-regulation as a tool to change someone, it's not going to work.

If your intention is to change the other person, how do you think that's going to go? If someone tried to change you through co-regulation, would that feel right? Or if they were simply a regulated person, without any intention to change you, would that feel different? I think it does. Co-regulation with intention is a distorted form of connection.

Yes, you're allowed to want that person to change. But when you share a smile with them, it's just to share a smile with them. Same with touching their arm, or lying next to them. It's a moment in time that you get to share. They will pick up on that naturally, and their body may lean more into regulating.

And co-regulation is not exactly enough. Yes, it can impact someone and bring them more into safety, but the shutdown is still there, even if it's less. It will still come and go. Eventually, the partner in shutdown needs to deal with their shutdown. Your genuine, spontaneous co-regulation will benefit them. It will help lay a foundation they need in order to then do something different and continue their own self-regulation process out of shutdown.
Basically, co-regulation is not something you can choose to use to make someone change. It's something you unintentionally offer when you are grounded in your safety state. Again, self-regulation.

So what's the real job for the partner of someone in shutdown? It's not about having the perfect response. It's not about saying the right thing or creating the perfect environment. Those things matter, but they're not the core of your job.

The core is: what's true for me right now? Can I be present without needing them to be different? Can I take care of my own nervous system? Can I be honest about my limits? Can I let their shutdown be what it is without making it mean something about me? Can I stay in the game, in the relationship, in the connection, without sacrificing myself?
That's the work. It's super difficult, and it's ongoing. It may lead you to very unpleasant but very honest answers. Maybe you do have a limit, as much as it pains you to admit it.

This dynamic in the relationship, and your own self-regulation efforts, are not a one-and-done solvable problem. It's a practice. Some days you'll nail it. Some days you'll be activated and frustrated, and you'll say something you wish you hadn't. Some days they'll come out of shutdown and things will feel better. Some days the shutdown is going to linger. Sometimes they'll come out of shutdown and into mobility, but spend it on video games or doom scrolling. That's all part of the picture.
I invite you to be honest with yourself every step of the way about how it's impacting you and your self-regulation efforts.

I think what's happening in relationships where one person experiences shutdown is that there's a lot of invisible pain on both sides. The person in shutdown is struggling with their own shutdown, their own capacity, their own disconnection. And the partner is struggling with helplessness, confusion, frustration, and maybe even a false sense of responsibility, and blame and shame toward themselves.

Both sides are real. But please know that you are not bad for being frustrated. You're not weak for being overwhelmed. You're not selfish for having boundaries. You're not failing by not being able to regulate your partner.

It's possible, and actually more likely, that if you can ground yourself, if you can be honest about your limits, if you can let go of the false responsibility and have healthy boundaries, you will show up differently. You'll be more present. And that presence, that realness, that groundedness: that's what co-regulation actually looks like.

So take care of you. Notice when you need to step back. Regulate your own nervous system, especially proactively, as part of a daily intentional practice. Set boundaries without guilt. Be honest about what you're struggling with. And let your person's shutdown be what it is: not a reflection of your love or your capacity, but a protective mechanism their body is using for now, even if it's been a long time.
